title: Hybrid Quantum-Classical Ensemble Learning for S&P 500 Directional Prediction
abstract_summary: This preprint proposes a hybrid quantum-classical ensemble for daily S&P 500 directional prediction that integrates a 4-qubit variational quantum circuit for sentiment feature extraction with diverse classical architectures (LSTM, Decision Transformer, XGBoost, Random Forest, Logistic Regression). The authors report that architecture diversity plus smart filtering (Top-7 selection) yields 60.14% directional accuracy on 2020–2023 data, with modest per-model gains from quantum features and statistically significant improvement over individual models.
methodology_description: This study implements a hybrid quantum-classical ensemble for daily S&P 500 directional prediction. The authors construct a 27-dimensional feature vector per day (25+ classical technical indicators plus a 1D quantum sentiment score) computed causally, and train five heterogeneous model families (LSTM, Decision Transformer, XGBoost, Random Forest, Logistic Regression) on seven financial instruments (S&P 500, VIX, Gold, XLF, XLK, HYG, IWM) for the period Jan 2020–Dec 2023 (1,006 trading days). A 4-qubit variational quantum circuit (VQC) is pre-trained on a supervised next-day-return task (parameters fixed afterwards) to produce a compact sentiment feature obtained by measuring Pauli-Z expectation values; the circuit is simulated with PennyLane’s default.qubit device. Models are trained with explicit hyperparameters (LSTM: seq length 5, two layers, 32/16 units, 15 epochs, Adam lr=1e-3; Decision Transformer: seq length 10, 2 transformer layers, 4 heads, 10 epochs; XGBoost/RandomForest/Logistic: specified tree counts and regularization), using a temporal 70/30 train-test split (704/302 days). They evaluate multiple aggregation strategies (Top-K majority voting with K=7 selected by validation accuracy, confidence-weighted voting, simple majority, dataset-specific ensembles, adaptive dynamic weighting) and employ a smart filter excluding base models with validation accuracy < 52% before aggregation. Evaluation uses directional accuracy, precision/recall, McNemar’s test for significance and Wilson score intervals; ablation studies measure ensemble and per-model impact of including the quantum feature.
algorithms_used: Variational Quantum Circuit (VQC) / Variational Quantum Algorithm (VQA)
experimental_setup: Experiments run on Google Colab using an NVIDIA T4 GPU. Quantum circuits are classically simulated using PennyLane's default.qubit device. Software stack: PennyLane 0.28, TensorFlow 2.10, scikit-learn 1.2, XGBoost 1.7.
dataset_used: Market-price time series covering Jan 2020–Dec 2023 (1,006 trading days) for seven instruments: S&P 500 (^GSPC), VIX, Gold futures (GC=F), Financial ETF (XLF), Technology ETF (XLK), High Yield Corporate Bond ETF (HYG), Russell 2000 ETF (IWM). Features per day include returns, log-returns, rolling volatilities (5/10/20), momentum (3/5/10), SMA/EMA (5/10/20), Bollinger Bands, RSI, and a quantum sentiment score; all features computed causally. Temporal train/test split 70%/30% (704/302 days).

experiment_input.source_note: Tickers listed in paper; exact data vendor not explicitly named (tickers imply common market data providers).
experiment_input.size: 1,006 trading days total; train = 704 days; test = 302 days.
experiment_input.preprocessing: Technical indicators computed causally (no lookahead). Quantum sentiment inputs: four normalized features (5-day avg return, 10-day volatility, 5-day momentum, current return) scaled to [0,1] before RY encoding. For tree methods the last 5 days of features are concatenated into a 135-d vector. Logistic regression features standardized; sequences prepared for LSTM (seq length 5) and Decision Transformer (seq length 10).

experiment_process: 1) Compute causal technical features for each trading day and normalize as required. 2) Pre-train a 4-qubit variational quantum circuit (two variational layers) on a supervised next-day-return task using parameter-shift gradients; freeze its parameters and extract a per-day quantum sentiment scalar by measuring average Pauli-Z expectations and applying a tanh transform. 3) Construct datasets for each instrument; for sequence models prepare sliding windows (LSTM=5, Decision Transformer=10). 4) Train 5 model families per instrument with stated hyperparameters: LSTM (32/16 units, dropout 0.3, Adam lr=1e-3, batch=32, 15 epochs), Decision Transformer (2 layers, 4 heads, dk=8, FFN 64, dropout 0.2, Adam lr=1e-3, 10 epochs), XGBoost (150 trees, max_depth=6, lr=0.1), RandomForest (150 trees, max_depth=15, sqrt(d) feature sampling), Logistic Regression (L2 C=0.1). 5) Evaluate models on validation, filter out models with validation accuracy < 52%. 6) Aggregate selected models via several ensemble strategies (Top-K majority voting with K=7 chosen by cross-validation, confidence-weighted voting, majority vote, adaptive 30-day performance weighting). 7) Perform ablation by retraining selected models without quantum sentiment to quantify impact. 8) Measure test accuracy, precision/recall; compute McNemar’s test for statistical significance and Wilson score intervals; conduct correlation analysis between model predictions and regime-based performance breakdown by VIX levels.
experiment_output: Primary metrics: directional accuracy (per-model and ensemble), precision and recall for positives, 95% Wilson confidence intervals, McNemar's test p-values comparing ensembles to baselines. Reported baseline: best individual model (VIX LSTM: 57.04%). Key reported outputs: Top-7 ensemble accuracy 60.14% (95% CI [56.84%,63.44%], p<0.05 vs best individual), ensemble without quantum features 59.32%, per-model accuracies across 35 combinations, ablation gains from quantum features (+0.78% to +1.50% per model), pairwise prediction correlations (same-architecture avg r≈0.61; different-architecture avg r≈0.38), regime accuracies by VIX bins, and preliminary backtest Sharpe ratio estimates (ensemble with confidence filtering: Sharpe ≈1.2 vs buy-and-hold 0.8).

quantum.measurement: Pauli-Z expectation per qubit, averaged and tanh-scaled
quantum.pretraining: quantum parameters pre-trained once on supervised next-day-return task and then frozen

Quantum circuit is simulated with PennyLane default.qubit (classical), which eases reproducibility. key_findings: [supported] The hybrid ensemble achieved 60.14% directional accuracy on 286 out-of-sample S&P 500 predictions (2020-2023).
[supported] The Top-7 filtered ensemble (selecting highest-performing models above a quality threshold) outperformed naive aggregation of all 35 trained models (60.14% vs. 51.20%).

[supported] Architecture diversity (combining different algorithms: LSTM, Decision Transformer, XGBoost, Random Forest, Logistic Regression) produced better ensemble performance than dataset diversity (different data sources with the same architecture): 57.34% vs. 52.80% in reported comparisons.

[supported] Same-architecture model predictions showed higher pairwise correlation (average r ≈ 0.61) than different-architecture models (average r ≈ 0.38), supporting the value of architectural heterogeneity for error decorrelation.

[supported] A 4-qubit variational quantum circuit (VQC) used as a sentiment/uncertainty feature extractor produced consistent per-model improvements in the range +0.78% to +1.50% across tested models (largest gains on volatility/VIX models).
[supported] Ablation comparing models with and without quantum-derived features showed ensemble accuracy of 60.14% with quantum features vs. 59.32% without (net +0.82%).

[supported] Statistical testing (McNemar's test) indicated the Top-7 ensemble improvement over the best individual model (VIX LSTM) is statistically significant (p < 0.05); 95% CI for ensemble accuracy reported as [56.84%, 63.44%].

[supported] Decision Transformer applied to financial prediction (no architecture-specific modifications) achieved competitive performance (56.99% on VIX), validating its applicability beyond RL tasks.
[supported] VIX/volatility-based prediction tasks were easier/predicted more accurately than direct price movement for some models; top individual models were VIX-based (e.g., VIX LSTM at 57.04%).
[supported] Smart filtering (excluding models below a 52% accuracy threshold) materially improved ensemble performance; the authors report that including weak predictors degraded results.

[supported] Regime analysis: ensemble accuracy varied by VIX regime and peaked in high-but-not-extreme volatility (VIX 25-35) at 66.67%, while performance degraded and became unstable during extreme volatility (VIX ≥ 35).

[supported] Computational feasibility claims: full pipeline (35 models) trained in ~45 minutes on commodity GPU (NVIDIA T4), per-model average training ≈1.3 minutes, ensemble inference latency ≈0.3 ms; quantum feature extraction overhead reported as <2% (PennyLane classical simulation).
[supported] Preliminary backtest with confidence-based filtering reported a Sharpe ratio ≈1.2 for the ensemble vs. 0.8 for buy-and-hold over the test period (authors note assumptions and caveats).

[speculative] The paper argues that quantum superposition provides a theoretical advantage for representing market uncertainty and that small VQCs are a pragmatic path to near-term quantum advantage in finance.

[speculative] The claim that the hybrid quantum-classical approach offers a near-term practical pathway to quantum advantage without fault-tolerant quantum computers is presented as a proposition rather than demonstrated on real quantum hardware.

[speculative] The quantum sentiment module’s conceptual mapping (encoding uncertainty via 4-qubit superposition/entanglement) is theoretical and not equivalent to demonstrating advantage on physical quantum hardware.
[supported] The quantum VQC parameters were pre-trained and then fixed during main model training to mitigate barren-plateau and optimization issues; quantum features were cached as classical inputs.
[speculative] The recommendation that expanding circuit size (e.g., to 8–12 qubits or more) could materially increase the quantum contribution is presented as future work / hypothesis.

[speculative] The suggestion that architecture diversity generally outweighs dataset diversity as a universal design principle for financial ensembles is asserted based on the presented experiments but may require broader validation across assets/periods.

[supported] The authors disclose limitations: the quantum module used classical simulation (PennyLane default.qubit), the experiment period is 2020–2023 and may not generalize to other regimes, and the small 4-qubit circuit has limited representational capacity.
results_summary: The preprint reports a hybrid quantum-classical ensemble for daily S&P 500 directional prediction that combines architectural diversity (LSTM, Decision Transformer, XGBoost, Random Forest, Logistic Regression), a small 4-qubit variational quantum sentiment feature, and smart quality filtering. On 286 out-of-sample days (2020–2023) the curated Top-7 ensemble achieved 60.14% directional accuracy (statistically significant vs. the best individual model), with modest but consistent per-model gains from the quantum-derived feature (+0.8%–1.5%). The study emphasizes that architecture heterogeneity and filtering out weak predictors drove performance gains; the quantum component was simulated classically and presented as a pragmatic, still speculative route toward near-term quantum benefit.

quantum_advantage_detail: The paper reports modest empirical gains from a classically-simulated 4-qubit variational circuit (+0.8%–1.5% per model) and frames the hybrid quantum-classical approach as a pragmatic pathway to near-term quantum advantage. However, no demonstration on physical quantum hardware or evidence of scaling to fault-tolerant quantum advantage is provided; the claims about quantum-specific representational advantage (superposition/entanglement modeling market uncertainty) remain theoretical/speculative given the small circuit, classical simulation, and limited effect sizes.

key_ideas: #idea:hybrid-approach — A practical hybrid pipeline: a 4-qubit variational quantum circuit (pre-trained and frozen) supplies a single daily 'quantum sentiment' scalar that augments classical technical indicators in heterogeneous ensembles (LSTM, Decision Transformer, XGBoost, Random Forest, Logistic Regression).

#idea:quantum-advantage — Inclusion of the simulated quantum sentiment yields modest per-model accuracy gains (+0.78% to +1.50%) and a small aggregate uplift in ensemble directional accuracy (Top-7 ensemble: 60.14% vs 59.32% without quantum feature), with reported statistical significance (McNemar p<0.05).

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Demonstrates a NISQ-scale experiment (4 qubits, 2 variational layers) simulated in PennyLane, arguing that small, pre-trained VQCs can produce useful compact features for classical ML pipelines.

#idea:hybrid-approach — Ensemble design and model-filtering (exclude base models <52% validation) and Top-K majority voting (K=7) are critical contributors to final performance; architecture diversity and smart filtering drive much of the ensemble gain.

#idea:quantum-advantage — The authors provide ablation studies attributing a modest but consistent incremental contribution from the quantum feature across multiple model families and instruments, and report auxiliary trading metrics (preliminary Sharpe improvements in backtest estimates).

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Methodological details: RY encoding of 4 normalized features into 4 qubits, circular CNOT entanglement, measurement of Pauli-Z expectations averaged and tanh-scaled, trained with parameter-shift gradients; parameters frozen after pretraining.

#idea:hybrid-approach — Extensive evaluation: temporal train/test split on Jan 2020–Dec 2023 market data (1,006 days), per-model hyperparameters, confidence intervals (Wilson), McNemar tests, regime breakdowns by VIX, and correlation analysis across model predictions.
contradictions: contradiction:classical-vs-quantum — The paper claims quantum-derived features improve prediction, but reported gains are small (sub-2% per model, ~0.8% ensemble uplift) and could plausibly arise from ensemble diversity and selection rather than uniquely quantum processing; no controlled comparison isolating quantum encoding vs. an equivalent classical compact feature is provided.

contradiction:scalability — The study uses a 4-qubit noiseless simulator and frozen small VQC; there is no evidence that the approach scales to larger feature sets, longer sequences, or noisy hardware, contradicting any implicit claims of broader quantum advantage or near-term deployability on QPUs.
